title_ar: شرح نخبة الفكر في مصطلح أهل الأثر -الشريط الخامس
title_en: Commentary on Nukhbat al-Fikr on the terminology of the people of hadith — tape five
body_ar: غير تعسف فهذا الذي يسمى بمختلف الحديث ومختلف الحديث هو ما ظاهره التعارض ولكن أهل العلم توصلوا إلى جمع بينه، فمثلا حديث ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال أيما إهاب دبغ فقد طهر، وحديث عبد الله بن عُكَيْمٍ أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أمرهم أن لا ينتفعوا من الميتة بجلد ولا عظم، هذان الحديثان ظاهرهما التعارض أن جلد الميتة طاهر بالدبغ في حديث ابن عباس، والنهي عن الانتفاع به مطلقا في حديث ابن عكيم، لكن قال بعض أهل العلم حديث ابن عباس فيه ذكر الإهاب وحديث ابن عكيم فيه ذكر الجلد، والإهاب هو ما دبغ والجلد ما لم يدبغ فجمعوا بينهما..
body_en: ...without forced interpretation. This is what is called the conflicting reports (mukhtalif al-ḥadīth). The conflicting reports are those whose apparent sense is in conflict, but which the people of knowledge have found a way to reconcile. For example, the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas, that the Prophet, upon whom be God's blessing and peace, said: "Any hide (ihāb) that is tanned has become pure"; and the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUkaym, that the Prophet, upon whom be God's blessing and peace, commanded them not to make use of anything from carrion, neither skin nor bone. These two hadiths are apparently in conflict: that the skin of carrion is pure by tanning, in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas; and the prohibition of making use of it without qualification, in the hadith of Ibn ʿUkaym. But some of the people of knowledge said: the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas mentions the ihāb, and the hadith of Ibn ʿUkaym mentions the jild, and the ihāb is what has been tanned and the jild is what has not been tanned. So they reconciled the two..

flags.context: the reconciliation of the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas with the hadith of Ibn ʿUkaym
options: translate as printed: the ihāb is what has been tanned and the jild is what has not been tanned
translate as printed and attach a reviewer's note that the received definition runs the other way
reverse the two terms to match the received definition
flags.note: PROBABLE SOURCE DEFECT, SUBSTANTIVE. The assignment of the two words here is the reverse of the one standardly reported in the hadith commentaries, where al-Nadr ibn Shumayl is quoted to the effect that ihāb is said of a skin that has NOT been tanned, and that once tanned it is no longer called ihāb — which is what makes the reconciliation work, since Ibn ʿAbbas's report speaks of an ihāb that is then tanned. As printed, the sentence makes Ibn ʿAbbas's wording redundant. This is most likely a slip in transcribing the spoken lecture rather than a position the Sheikh holds. Under the rule against silently repairing the source it has been translated as printed; option 2 is set out only to be rejected. A reviewer with the audio should settle it, and it should be settled before publication, because as it stands the passage attributes a demonstrably odd lexical claim to the Sheikh.

translator_notes: Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The date shown by the CMS is a bulk-upload timestamp shared by every item in this range, not the date the Sheikh gave the answer. The real date of composition is unknown. See date_is_cms_bulk_upload.

This record belongs to the Sheikh's commentary on Ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani's Nukhbat al-Fikr, a short manual of hadith terminology. The CMS holds the tapes out of order across ids 628–637 and the tape numbers in the titles do not run with the ids; the series should be ordered by the tape number in the title, not by id, and even then a gap remains (see the note on the download filenames).

EXCERPT ONLY. The published text is the opening of a lecture and breaks off; the full transcript is offered as a .docx download ('taḥmīl al-māddah'). The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. The download-link label has been removed from body_ar as a navigation element and recorded in source_download_link.
'Forced interpretation' renders taʿassuf — straining a text to remove an apparent conflict. The condition the excerpt opens on is that a reconciliation must not be forced.
'Carrion' renders maytah, an animal that has died otherwise than by lawful slaughter.
'Pure' renders ṭahara, ritual purity of a substance, not validity and not moral status.
Both hadiths are given without a named collection and without a grading. None has been supplied.
